opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find most significant about that work is that it challenges a really deeply held assumption in our field, which is that more data is always better. For a long time, the default recipe for pretraining has been to scrape as much of the web as you can and throw compute at it. What we asked instead was: can we be much more deliberate about what the model actually sees, and can removing data make the model better rather than worse?

And the interesting finding is that yes, you can prune quite aggressively. We looked at different ways of estimating data quality at scale, things like perplexity-based scoring, where you use a reference model to rank examples, as well as other heuristics people commonly use, like error-based or memorization-based signals. What was surprising is that a fairly simple approach, perplexity scoring, held up really well, and in some cases training on a fraction of the original dataset matched or even outperformed training on the full thing.

I think there are a few reasons that matters. One is efficiency. If you can get the same or better performance with substantially less data, that's less compute, lower cost, and a smaller environmental footprint. That makes this kind of research more accessible to people outside of a handful of very well-resourced labs.

The second is that it reframes data as a lever we've been underusing. So much of the attention in the field goes to architecture changes or scaling parameters, but the quality and composition of the data is arguably just as important. Web-scale corpora are really noisy, with a lot of duplication, low-quality text, and boilerplate, and the model is spending capacity on all of it.

And the third thing, which I find intellectually exciting, is that it opens up questions about what "quality" even means for a model. A human might judge text one way, but what's useful for a model's learning might be quite different. Some of the nuance we saw was that which slice of the distribution you keep, for example the middle versus the extremes of the perplexity ranking, really matters. That tells us we're still at an early stage of understanding the relationship between data and generalization, and I think that's where a lot of the most interesting work in the next few years is going to come from.

r002.rationale: It says pruning can reduce the amount of data while maintaining performance, but does not say the retained examples can be seen more times during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think what's really interesting about that paper is that it pushes back on an assumption that has quietly become dogma in how we pretrain large language models, which is that more data is always better, and that the right way to deal with data is essentially to hoover up as much of the web as you can, apply some fairly crude heuristic filters, deduplicate, and then train on whatever is left.

What "Less Is More" does, and it builds on a lot of prior work in the data pruning space, including some of our own, is ask a much more pointed question: of the tokens you have, which ones are actually contributing to learning, and can you be far more aggressive about throwing data away than people have been comfortable with? And the headline result is that you can prune a substantial fraction of the pretraining corpus and either match or in some cases improve downstream performance.

There are a couple of things I find significant about it. The first is the scoring mechanism. Rather than relying purely on surface-level heuristics, things like document length or perplexity under a reference model, they use signals that are more tightly coupled to the model's own learning dynamics. Perplexity-based pruning has always been a bit of a double-edged sword, because low perplexity can mean "high quality" but it can also mean "boring and redundant," and high perplexity can mean "noisy garbage" or it can mean "genuinely novel and informative." So any method that gets better at disentangling those is valuable.

The second thing, and this is the one I care about most, is what it says about the economics of scale. We're in a regime where compute is the bottleneck for most labs outside of a handful of very well-resourced players. If you can show that a carefully curated dataset at a fraction of the size gets you equivalent performance, that's not just an efficiency story, that's an access story. It changes who can participate in training frontier-adjacent models. And it shifts investment away from "acquire more tokens" toward "understand the tokens you already have," which I think is the healthier direction for the field.

The third thing I'd flag is more of a caution than a celebration. Any time you prune, you're making a decision about what gets to count as valuable data, and those decisions are not neutral. Our work on data pruning found pretty consistently that aggressive pruning tends to disproportionately remove examples from the tail of the distribution, which often means underrepresented languages, dialects, or rarer topics. So when I read a paper like this I'm always looking not just at the aggregate benchmark numbers but at what's being lost, and whether the evaluation suite is rich enough to even detect that loss. Average performance holding steady can mask a lot of redistribution underneath.

So I'd summarize it as: a genuinely important contribution to the idea that data is a first-class lever in model design, not just an input you scale up, but one where the next step has to be a more careful accounting of who the pruned data would have served.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that it challenges the assumption that more data is always better. In pretraining, we tend to treat dataset size as a proxy for value, but examples aren’t equally useful. There’s redundancy, and there’s a question of how much additional learning each example actually provides.

Data pruning makes that question explicit: can we be more deliberate about what we train on and get comparable—or better—performance with less computation? That’s significant because it makes data selection part of the recipe for scaling, rather than simply increasing the volume.

The caveat I’d emphasize is that usefulness isn’t necessarily universal. An example that looks unnecessary for average benchmark performance might matter a great deal for a particular language or a less represented group. So I’d want to understand both the efficiency gains and what capabilities are preserved or lost.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find significant is that it challenges the assumption that more data is always better. With pretraining, we tend to focus on scale, but the composition of the data matters enormously. Pruning makes that question explicit: which examples are actually contributing to what the model learns?

The difficult part is deciding what counts as useful. An example might look redundant or unhelpful according to your selection criterion and still represent something rare that you want the model to learn. So I’m interested in both the efficiency opportunity and the distributional consequences. If you can train with less data, that’s valuable—but you also want to understand whose performance improves and what capabilities you might be losing.
